name: Drones for Agricultural Monitoring 6: Online Drone Piloting Course
objectives: Using a drone controller or simulator, name what each stick movement does and read the main items on the flight screen, and find the return-to-home and pause buttons without looking
In a drone simulator, fly the hover, box, figure eight, orbit and lawnmower drills and record every session in a log book, flying each drill smoothly three times in a row
When GPS is strong or weak, explain the main flight modes and fly calmly when the drone drops into attitude mode, keeping the drone in sight and landing safely

lessons.title: Lesson 1: The controls: sticks, buttons and screen
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Name what each stick movement does and read the main items on the flight screen.
This lesson builds toward: Using a drone controller or simulator, you will name what each stick movement does and read the main items on the flight screen, and find the return-to-home and pause buttons without looking.
Most drone controllers have two sticks. In Mode 2, the most common setup, the left stick controls height (throttle: up to climb, down to descend) and turning on the spot (yaw: left and right). The right stick moves the drone forward and back (pitch) and sideways (roll). Some pilots use other modes; check yours in the app settings.
Small, smooth stick movements make smooth flight. Beginners push too far and too fast. Practise moving the sticks gently, then letting them return to centre, where most drones hold position.
The flight screen shows battery level, signal strength, GPS satellites, height, distance from home and the camera view. Learn to glance at it, then look back at the drone. Know where the return-to-home and pause or brake buttons are without looking.
Words to know:
- Throttle: up and down movement (climb or descend).
- Yaw: turning the drone left or right on the spot.
- Pitch: moving forward or back.
- Roll: moving sideways left or right.
- Mode 2: the most common stick setup: left stick throttle and yaw, right stick pitch and roll.
Try it now: Install a drone simulator on a computer or phone (search your app store or computer for a drone flight simulator; some drone makers offer one in their app). Find the stick mode setting, set Mode 2, and move each stick gently to see what it does.
You can now say what each stick does in Mode 2, read the flight screen, and find the emergency buttons.

options: Moving the drone forward and back
check.why: Pitch moves the drone forward and back; in Mode 2 it is on the right stick.

check.q: Your drone is drifting towards a tree and you must stop it fast. What should you already know?
options: How to change the camera colour
Where the pause or brake button is, without looking
check.why: Pilots learn where the pause or brake and return-to-home buttons are so they can act without looking.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Practice drills in a simulator
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Fly five standard drills smoothly in a simulator.
This lesson builds toward: In a drone simulator, you will fly the hover, box, figure eight, orbit and lawnmower drills and record every session in a log book, flying each drill smoothly three times in a row.
Good pilots build skill with the same drills, many times. Practise each drill until you can fly it smoothly three times in a row, then move on. Short daily sessions of 15 to 20 minutes work better than one long session a week.
Drill 1, hover: take off to eye height and hold the drone still for one minute. Drill 2, box: fly a square with the nose always facing forward, then again with the nose turning at each corner. Drill 3, figure eight: fly a smooth figure eight. Drill 4, orbit: circle a point (such as a tree) while keeping the camera on it. Drill 5, lawnmower: fly straight parallel lines across a field, like a mapping flight, by hand.
Also practise with the drone facing you (nose-in), when left and right feel reversed. This is where most beginners crash. After each session, write what went well and what to improve.
Step by step:
- Hover at eye height for one minute.
- Box: nose forward, then nose turning at corners.
- Figure eight, smooth and level.
- Orbit a tree with the camera on it.
- Lawnmower lines across a field.
- Repeat each one nose-in.
Words to know:
- Drill: a short exercise repeated to build a skill.
- Nose-in: flying with the front of the drone facing you, so controls feel reversed.
- Orbit: flying in a circle around a point.
Try it now: In your simulator, fly drills 1 and 2 today. Write in a notebook: date, minutes, which drills, how many smooth runs, one thing to improve.
You can now practise five standard drills in a simulator and track your progress.

options: Flying a square, first with the nose forward, then turning at each corner
check.why: The box drill flies a square with the nose facing forward, then with the nose turning at each corner.

check.q: You have flown the hover drill smoothly once. What do you do next?
options: Keep practising until it is smooth three times in a row, then move on
check.why: Practise each drill until you can fly it smoothly three times in a row.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Flight modes and when to use them
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Explain the main flight modes and switch safely when GPS is weak.
This lesson builds toward: When GPS is strong or weak, you will explain the main flight modes and fly calmly when the drone drops into attitude mode, keeping the drone in sight and landing safely.
Most camera drones fly in a positioning or GPS mode. The drone uses satellites and sensors to hold its place when you let go of the sticks, which makes flying easier and allows return-to-home and automatic mapping.
Some drones also have an attitude mode (some brands call it ATTI). The drone holds its height but not its place, so it drifts with the wind like a boat on a river. A drone can drop into this mode by itself when GPS is weak, for example near tall metal structures, under thick trees, or in a deep valley. Pilots who have practised it stay calm; those who have not often crash.
Other modes include sport (faster, less protection), tripod or cine (slow and smooth for filming), and automatic missions. Many simulators let you fly without GPS help. Practise it so drift does not surprise you.
Words to know:
- GPS mode: a flight mode where the drone uses satellites to hold its place.
- Attitude mode (ATTI): a mode where the drone holds height but drifts with the wind.
- Drift: the drone moving away by itself, usually with the wind.
Try it now: In your simulator, switch off GPS help or choose attitude mode, add some wind, and hold a hover for 30 seconds by correcting drift. Then fly the box drill in this mode.
You can now explain the main flight modes and keep control when the drone drifts without GPS.

check.q: What does tripod or cine mode do?
options: Flies slowly and smoothly for filming
check.why: Tripod or cine mode is slow and smooth, for filming.

check.q: You will map a field next to a tall metal grain silo. What do you prepare for?
options: The drone dropping into attitude mode and drifting, so you practise flying without GPS help
check.why: Near tall metal structures GPS can be weak, and the drone may drift in attitude mode.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Emergency drills: lost link, low battery, GPS loss
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Follow the right steps in three common emergencies.
This lesson builds toward: In a simulated lost link, low battery or GPS loss, you will follow the right emergency steps, calmly and in the right order, then logging the event.
Emergencies are rare but fast. Pilots handle them well because they have practised the steps until they are automatic. Before each real flight, check that return-to-home height and the action on lost signal are set correctly.
Lost link (the controller loses signal): stay calm, point the controller's antennas towards the drone, move to a higher spot if safe. Most drones start return-to-home after a few seconds; watch the sky and be ready to take control when the link returns. Low battery: stop the task and fly home directly, or land at the nearest safe spot; never try to finish one more line.
GPS loss or sudden drift: switch your mind to attitude flying, keep the drone in sight, fly it gently back towards you against the wind, and land as soon as it is safe. After any emergency or crash, make the area safe, check for damage, write it in your log book, and report it to the authority if your rules require.
Step by step:
- Lost link: stay calm, point antennas, move higher if safe, watch for return-to-home.
- Low battery: stop the task, fly home or land at the nearest safe spot.
- GPS loss: fly gently by hand, against the wind, land soon.
- After any incident: make safe, check damage, log it, report if required.
Words to know:
- Lost link: when the drone and controller lose their radio connection.
- Fly-away: when a drone flies off out of the pilot's control.
- Incident: an unplanned event that caused, or could have caused, harm or damage.
Official sources:
- Nigeria Civil Aviation Authority (NCAA): Nig.CARs 2023 Part 21, Remotely Piloted Aircraft Systems
- Kenya Civil Aviation Authority (KCAA): Unmanned Aircraft Systems
Try it now: In your simulator, practise each emergency: set a low-battery warning and fly home, switch off GPS mid-flight and land by hand, and (if the simulator allows) trigger a signal loss and watch return-to-home. Write the steps from memory afterwards.
You can now follow the right steps for lost link, low battery and GPS loss.

check.q: Before every real flight, what do you check to prepare for a lost link?
options: That return-to-home height and the lost-signal action are set correctly
check.why: Correct return-to-home height and lost-signal action let the drone come home safely if the link is lost.

check.q: After a hard landing with a real drone, it looks fine. What do you do?
options: Check it for damage and write it in the log book
Fly again at once without checking
check.why: After any emergency or crash, check for damage and log it; report it if the rules require.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Keeping a pilot log book
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Record every simulator and real flight in a log book.
This lesson builds toward: In a drone simulator, you will fly the hover, box, figure eight, orbit and lawnmower drills and record every session in a log book, flying each drill smoothly three times in a row.
A log book is your flying record. Training organisations and aviation authorities use flight logs to check experience, and employers and clients trust pilots who keep them. Keep simulator time and real flight time in separate columns.
For each session record: date, place (or simulator), drone or simulator name, total minutes, type of flying (drills, mapping, inspection), conditions (wind, light), any problems or incidents, and what you learned. For real flights also note the registration of the drone and any approval used.
Use a paper notebook, a spreadsheet or a logging app, but keep it every time and back it up. Ask your training organisation which format it accepts for licence applications.
Step by step:
- Choose paper, spreadsheet or app, and back it up.
- Separate columns for simulator and real flights.
- Record date, place, aircraft, minutes, type, conditions, problems, lessons.
- For real flights, add registration and approval used.
- Ask your training organisation which format it accepts.
Words to know:
- Log book: a record of every flight a pilot makes.
- Flight time: the minutes or hours a pilot has spent flying.
Try it now: Start your log book now as a spreadsheet with the columns from this lesson, and enter every simulator session you have done in this course so far.
You can now keep a complete pilot log book for simulator and real flights.

check.q: Why do training organisations and authorities look at flight logs?
check.why: Flight logs show a pilot's experience to schools, authorities, employers and clients.

check.q: You flew a real drone today under an approval. What do you add to the log entry?
options: The drone's registration and the approval used
check.why: For real flights, also note the drone's registration and any approval used.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Your path to a remote pilot licence
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Write a personal plan to earn a remote pilot licence in your country.
This lesson builds toward: For your country, you will write a personal plan to earn a remote pilot licence, with the authority, approved schools, steps, documents, costs from official sources and target dates.
Each country decides how remote pilots are licensed. In Kenya, KCAA approves Unmanned Aircraft Systems Training Organizations (UTOs) and lists them on its website; its fee schedule includes a student remote pilot licence, a remote pilot licence (RPL) and extra ratings such as beyond visual line of sight. Applications run through KCAA's online drone system. In Nigeria, NCAA's Part 21 sets out remote pilot licensing and other RPAS requirements. Other countries have their own rules.
The usual path: choose an approved training organisation; study the theory (air law, airspace and maps, weather, the aircraft, human factors, emergency procedures); take flying lessons and a practical test; pass the authority's requirements; apply for the licence; and keep it valid by renewing it as required.
Check every step, document and fee on the authority's official pages or by calling it, and check that a school is on the authority's approved list before you pay. Your simulator log shows you are ready to learn fast, but it does not replace approved training.
Step by step:
- Find your aviation authority's drone pages.
- Find its list of approved training organisations; pick two to contact.
- Ask each: course length, theory and practical content, cost, test, documents needed.
- Check the licence fee on the official fee schedule.
- Write target dates for training, test and application.
Words to know:
- Approved training organisation: a drone school approved by the aviation authority to train pilots for a licence (KCAA calls them UTOs).
- Rating: an extra permission on a licence for a type of flying, such as beyond visual line of sight.
- Air law: the rules about flying and airspace.
Official sources:
- KCAA: Unmanned Aircraft Systems Training Organizations (UTO)
- KCAA drone (RPAS) online system
- Kenya Civil Aviation Authority (KCAA): Unmanned Aircraft Systems
- Nigeria Civil Aviation Authority (NCAA): Nig.CARs 2023 Part 21, Remotely Piloted Aircraft Systems
Try it now: Final task: finish the five drills and three emergency drills in your simulator, keep every session in your log book, and write your one-page licensing plan: authority, approved schools found, licence needed, steps, documents, cost from official sources, and target dates.
You can now fly standard drills and emergency procedures in a simulator, keep a log book, and follow a clear plan to an official remote pilot licence.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Five drills One or more drills are not yet smooth three times in a row. Hover, box, figure eight, orbit and lawnmower each flown smoothly three times in a row. Also flies the box and figure eight smoothly nose-in. Emergency drills Panics or skips steps in an emergency drill. Follows the right steps for lost link, low battery and GPS loss. Lands safely from attitude mode against the wind without help. Log book Sessions are missing or entries lack key fields. Every session logged with date, simulator, minutes, type, conditions, problems and lessons. Simulator and real time are in separate columns and the log is backed up. Licensing plan The authority, licence or steps are missing, or costs are guessed. Authority, approved schools found, licence needed, steps, documents, cost from official sources and target dates. Has contacted a school on the approved list and noted the date checked. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, practise or fix that part and check it again.

check.q: Which is a usual step on the path to a remote pilot licence?
options: Training at an approved organisation, then a practical test
check.why: The usual path is approved training, theory, flying lessons and a test, then the licence application.

check.q: A website offers a remote pilot licence online in one day with no test, for a fee. What do you do?
options: Pay quickly before the offer ends
Check the authority's official pages and approved list before paying anything
check.why: Licences come from the aviation authority; check that a school is on its approved list before you pay.
